A recent study conducted by the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) has revealed significant concerns among Scottish small businesses regarding potential future skills shortages, particularly in the context of Brexit. The findings indicate that two-thirds of small Scottish firms with EU staff are apprehensive about the prospect of skill shortages. Moreover, 37% of these businesses stated that they would consider reducing their operations if Brexit results in additional barriers to hiring EU citizens. Additionally, almost one-fifth of the surveyed firms indicated a possibility of closing their businesses, with 12% considering relocation to other countries.

The FSB's research underscores the crucial role that EU workers play in addressing chronic skills gaps across various sectors. Specifically, 26% of Scottish small employers currently employ EU staff, a figure that rises to 41% in the Highlands. In comparison, only about one-fifth of UK firms have EU workers on their payroll. The survey also found that nearly 90% of respondents recruited their EU staff while they were already residing in the UK. Importantly, the majority of UK respondents (95%) reported having no experience with the UK's points-based immigration system for recruiting non-EU workers.

Leicestershire Fire and Rescue services have successfully contained the fire, although teams remain on-site to ensure safety.

Western Power engineers are actively working to restore electricity at the earliest opportunity. During the crisis, residents affected by evacuations were directed to the Belgrave Neighbourhood Centre on Rothley Street, which had been established as an emergency refuge.

At the peak of the fire, water was extracted from a nearby canal to assist firefighting efforts, while police managed crowds due to hazardous smoke emissions. Fortunately, there have been no reported injuries associated with the incident. The smoke from the fire was visible as far as Bradgate Park, approximately five miles (8 km) away. Authorities continue to monitor the situation closely and will provide updates as necessary.

This influx of workers is attributed to an increase in the number of workers from other EU countries, as well as older workers and individuals previously receiving welfare benefits.

The application offers real-time updates when connected to Wi-Fi, ensuring that users receive the most current information promptly. Additionally, it remains functional offline. Health Secretary Shona Robison highlighted that this app, developed collaboratively with healthcare professionals and patients, facilitates expedited access to crucial referral information for suspected cancer cases among doctors, pharmacists, and senior nurses. Early diagnosis and treatment of cancer significantly improve survival rates; hence, increasing the proportion of early-stage diagnoses will likely reduce cancer-related premature mortality and positively impact overall life expectancy. Consequently, she strongly encourages all pertinent healthcare practitioners to download and utilize this invaluable tool.

Dr. Douglas Rigg, a general practitioner from Glasgow who contributed to the app's development, emphasized that it provides rapid access to essential information supporting clinical decision-making. As mobile devices become indispensable in general practice settings, applications like this are poised to play a pivotal role in the future of primary care by helping GPs maintain current knowledge.

A brain scan conducted by neurosurgeon Soren Singel revealed the presence of a tapeworm larva, which Ortiz was informed was highly lethal, giving him a prognosis of approximately 30 minutes to live. The larva resided within a cyst that had obstructed circulation and water supply to the remainder of Ortiz’s brain. “I stood up and then I threw up,” Ortiz recounted, “and the doctor pulled it out, saying it was still wiggling; at that moment, I thought it couldn’t get much worse.”

Neurocysticercosis, a condition caused by larval cysts of the tapeworm, typically develops when a person ingests microscopic eggs expelled in the feces of an individual harboring an intestinal pork tapeworm. Once ingested, these eggs can hatch within the human body and migrate to the brain, establishing cysts that may interfere with cerebral blood flow and neural function.

Gentoo, a housing association, has proactively removed cladding from several buildings as a precautionary measure following the Grenfell Tower tragedy, where it is believed 79 people lost their lives. To date, 60 buildings across 25 council areas have failed combustibility tests. In Sunderland, the affected properties with cladding removed include Zetland, Church North, Dock, Dame Dorothy, and the Victor block of flats. 

Gentoo clarified that none of its buildings utilized the same cladding as Grenfell Tower. However, the decision to remove the cladding was made to reassure residents about their safety. In a statement, the company explained: "We have taken the precautionary step of removing a small amount of decorative paneling from five of our blocks in the St Peter's area. Additionally, we are conducting face-to-face reassurance meetings with our residents to ensure their ongoing safety."

An elderly resident on the 13th floor of the Victor building, who wished to remain anonymous, expressed his confidence in Gentoo's commitment to safety, noting that "Gentoo is always doing things to keep the residents happy."

In related news, a petition has been initiated urging the owners of another student accommodation block to disclose whether their building is affected by similar issues. St James Point, owned by Brookfield Student Real Estate, accommodates 80 Newcastle University students and over 200 other students. A spokesperson for the company stated that the building adheres to the highest fire safety standards.

Steph Mosley from Acorn, an advocacy group for renters' rights, voiced concerns about the uncertainty surrounding the cladding materials: "We don't know what is in the cladding. The echolocation capabilities of marine mammals, such as porpoises, whales, and dolphins, are integral to their hunting strategies. These animals emit clicks and buzzes to locate their prey, and they rely on the echoes that return from the targets. Researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark have elucidated a fascinating acoustic behavior: as these animals home in on their prey, they transition from a narrow to a wide beam of sound. This transition is analogous to adjusting a flashlight to better illuminate a target.

This adaptive beam-steering technique could enhance the hunting efficiency of these marine mammals, potentially making it more difficult for their prey to evade capture. Furthermore, understanding these acoustic behaviors could lead to innovative methods for preventing porpoises and other toothed whales from becoming inadvertently entangled in fishing nets.

To investigate this phenomenon, the research team conducted a series of experiments with harbor porpoises in a semi-natural enclosure located along the Danish coast. The enclosure was designed to simulate a more natural environment while still allowing for detailed acoustic monitoring. Harbor porpoises were equipped with sound-detecting tags, and numerous microphones were deployed around the enclosure to capture acoustic data. Mr. Pernetti acknowledged that it was ultimately his decision to attempt rehabilitation, but now concedes that this approach was misguided.

In an attempt to challenge municipal regulations, Uber and Lyft sought to overturn a city council mandate requiring drivers to undergo fingerprint-based background checks before being allowed to operate. However, these regulations—initially enacted in December 2015—were upheld following a public referendum. Both companies expressed their disappointment with the outcome. The rules aimed to align ride-sharing services with the standards traditionally applied to taxi operators, ensuring a consistent level of oversight across the industry. According to National Public Radio (NPR), Uber invested approximately $8 million (£5.5 million) in support of Proposition One, a campaign advocating for self-regulation rather than compliance with the council’s requirements. Despite this substantial effort, 55% of the 87,212 votes cast were against the proposition. Reflecting on this outcome, Chris Nakutis, Uber Austin's General Manager, stated: “Disappointment does not begin to describe how we feel about shutting down operations in Austin. We hope the city council will reconsider their ordinance so we can collaborate to make Austin’s streets safer for everyone.” At the time of reporting, Uber continued to display fare estimates for rides within the city, despite ceasing operations. Lyft expressed similar dissatisfaction, asserting that the regulations impede authentic ride-sharing practices. The company highlighted that these rules disproportionately affect part-time drivers—the cornerstone of Lyft’s peer-to-peer business model—by making it more difficult for them to participate, while simultaneously limiting passenger access to rides. "Instead," Lyft emphasized, "they create barriers for both drivers and riders alike." During initial discussions about the proposed regulations, Austin Mayor Steve Adler conveyed a neutral stance, stating: “Ultimately our goal is not to favor any particular company’s presence or absence.” This sentiment was reported by *The Texas Tribune*. The report, *Caught Short*, highlights that India is home to at least 48 million stunted children under the age of five. This figure places India second only to Nigeria and Pakistan, which together account for 10.3 and 9.8 million stunted children, respectively. Stunting, a condition primarily resulting from malnutrition during the critical first two years of life, is largely irreversible and significantly impacts both physical and cognitive development. Besides food shortages, several additional factors contribute to this issue, including poor sanitation and contaminated drinking water, which exacerbate malnutrition and subsequently stunted growth.

The report further underscores that inadequate access to sanitation, clean water, and hygiene practices plays a crucial role in the prevalence of stunting. Repeated episodes of diarrhea, often attributed to polluted water sources and unhygienic environments, are closely associated with malnutrition. Diarrhea is estimated to account for approximately one-quarter of all cases of stunting, especially in the initial years of a child's life. Additionally, the report reveals that over 76 million people in India live without safe drinking water, and an alarming 774 million individuals lack adequate sanitation facilities. Reflecting on the momentous occasion, Hugill stated, "We were acutely aware of the significance of the day, yet the extensive preparatory work undertaken by the team ensured that there was no sense of nervousness among us; everyone understood their assigned tasks." 

Ms. Hugill expressed profound honor at being recognized for her service. She enlisted in the Women's Royal Naval Service (Wrens) in 1942, initially serving as a typist.
